extracted.intended_audience: aspiring storytellers, essayists, poets, and stage actors (literary/performing practitioners and critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing and delivering stories, poems, and stage performances: how to use surprise, diction, plausibility, voice, gesture, and persona to move or amuse an audience. Draws on examples from essays, poetry criticism, and acting precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprize is the Life of Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprize is so much the Life of Stories, that every one aims at it, who endeavours to please by telling them. Smooth Delivery, an elegant Choice of Words, and a sweet Arrangement, are all beautifying Graces, but not the particulars in this Point of Conversation which either long command the Attention, or strike with the Violence of a sudden Passion, or occasion the burst of Laughter which accompanies Humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprise (a sudden turn, unexpected detail or punch) as the principal engine of a tale to seize attention, provoke strong emotion, or produce laughter. While good diction and arrangement are important 'beautifying graces', they do not replace the necessity of a well-timed or well-placed surprise. The traveller/seat analogy: first view gives instant delight — don't make the audience have to labor through what a single striking moment could achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid outraging truth / over-leaping the line of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Set of Men who outrage Truth, instead of affecting us with a Manner in telling it; who over-leap the Line of Probability, that they may be seen to move out of the common Road; and endeavour only to make their Hearers stare, by imposing upon them with a kind of Nonsense against the Philosophy of Nature, or such a Heap of Wonders told upon their own Knowledge, as it is not likely one Man should ever have met with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain plausibility in stories. Avoid piling improbable wonders or nonsense merely to astonish; such devices tend to expose the teller and alienate the audience. The text gives comic examples (miraculous effects of cheeses, eccentric antipathies) to show how implausible claims become targets for ridicule rather than admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth delivery, elegant diction, and arrangement are necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Smooth Delivery, an elegant Choice of Words, and a sweet Arrangement, are all beautifying Graces, but not the particulars ... which either long command the Attention, or strike with the Violence of a sudden Passion, or occasion the burst of Laughter which accompanies Humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate polished language, careful phrasing, and clear structure as foundational qualities, but remember they adorn rather than replace the core elements (surprise, strong emotional turns) that keep an audience engaged. Avoid relying on style alone to carry weak material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret and manage audience reaction (silence vs opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first of these is a general Silence, which I would not advise any one to interpret in his own behalf. ... Silence, or a negligent Indifference, proceeds from Anger, mixed with a Scorn that shews another he is thought by you too contemptible to be regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read audience silence carefully—often it signals contempt, prudence, or refusal to engage rather than credulous acceptance. Opposition (contradiction) implies the speaker is still considered worth contesting; silence can wound more deeply. Use this social information to moderate claims and to repair credibility when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose or correct implausible tellers by mimicry/over-shooting
rubrics_metrics.description: The other Method which the World has taken for correcting this Practice of false Surprize, is to over-shoot such Talkers in their own Bow, or to raise the Story with further Degrees of Impossibility, and set up for a Voucher to them in such a manner as must let them see they stand detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical corrective to boastful/unbelievable storytellers is to parody or amplify their improbabilities until the absurdity is plain. Mimicry acts as social pedagogy: imitate their manner/claim to make them recognise how they appear, shaming them without blunt confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present great works as they are — avoid self-indulgent additions
rubrics_metrics.description: If we must be entertained with the Works of any of those great Men, desire these Gentlemen to give them us as they find them, that so, when we read them to our Families at home, they may the better remember they have heard them at Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When repeating or presenting canonical material (sermons, great texts), do not tack on personal embellishments aimed at displaying ingenuity. Such additions can distract from the original's force and irritate audiences who expect fidelity; preserve the integrity of notable passages when your purpose is instruction or remembrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personae / pseudonymous letters as a literary device
rubrics_metrics.description: I often chuse this way of casting my Thoughts into a Letter ... First, out of the Policy of those who try their Jest upon another, before they own it themselves. Secondly, because I would extort a little Praise from such who will never applaud any thing whose Author is known and certain. Thirdly, because it gave me an Opportunity of introducing a great variety of Characters into my Work, which could not have been done, had I always written in the Person of the Spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting fictional correspondents or masks can be a deliberate technique to diversify voice, to test audience reaction, and to obtain commentary or praise that might not be forthcoming under the author's own name. Use personae to introduce varied perspectives, regional voices, or comic types, but be mindful of the rhetorical purpose for masking authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical plan and unity in moral/epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's general Plan is the Representation of six Virtues, Holiness, Temperance, Chastity, Friendship, Justice and Courtesy, in six Legends by six Persons. The six Personages are supposed under proper Allegories suitable to their respective Characters, to do all that is necessary for the full Manifestation of the respective Virtues which they are to exert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing moral or allegorical poems, ensure the overarching plan supports distinct virtues/themes, and that each sub-narrative or legend fully embodies and demonstrates its assigned virtue. Maintain coherence between allegory and action so the structure elucidates rather than obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction and style: avoid puns, affectations, and forced antitheses
rubrics_metrics.description: His stile is very Poetical; no Puns, Affectations of Wit, forced Antitheses, or any of that low Tribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor genuine imagery and apt expression over cheap verbal trickery. Avoid puns, artificial cleverness, or strained contrasts that call attention to the poet's wit rather than the poem's feeling. Use words (including archaic words where appropriate) that suit the poem's dignity and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of epithets and varied imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer's Epithets were much admired by Antiquity: See what great Justness and Variety there is in these Epithets of the Trees in the Forest where the Red-cross Knight lost Truth ... 'The sailing Pine, the Cedar proud and tall, The Vine-prop Elm, the Poplar never dry, The Builder Oak, sole King of Forests all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epithets and images that are both varied and fitting to the object described; apt descriptive tags add texture and mnemonic force. Study classical exemplars for how concise epithets can conjure vivid particulars without obscuring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice modulation matched to emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature herself has assigned to every Emotion of the Soul, its peculiar Cast of the Countenance, Tone of Voice, and Manner of Gesture. ... Anger exerts its peculiar Voice in an acute, raised, and hurrying sound. Sorrow and Complaint demand a Voice quite different, flexible, slow, interrupted, and modulated in a mournful Tone. Fear expresses itself in a low, hesitating and abject Sound. Courage assumes a louder tone. Pleasure dissolves into a luxurious, mild, tender, and joyous Modulation. Perplexity is different ... grave, but not bemoaning, with an earnest uniform Sound of Voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train vocal variety so that each emotion has its characteristic pitch, tempo, and quality. Use acute/rapid tones for anger, slow/interrupted tones for sorrow, low/hesitant tones for fear, loud/resolute tones for courage, mild/tender tones for pleasure, and even/earnest tones for perplexity. Illustrative passages (Lear, Wolsey, Lady Macbeth, Hamlet) demonstrate these contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action/gesture must be directed by the voice and the sense
rubrics_metrics.description: As all these Varieties of Voice are to be directed by the Sense, so the Action is to be directed by the Voice ... The Arm ... is to be sometimes raised and extended; and the Hand, by its Motion, sometimes to lead, and sometimes to follow the Words, as they are uttered. The Stamping of the Foot too has its proper Expression in Contention, Anger, or absolute Command. But the Face is the Epitome of the whole Man, and the Eyes are as it were the Epitome of the Face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate gesture with vocal emphasis and semantic sense. Use arm and hand purposefully (lead or follow speech), employ foot-stamping for command or anger, and use facial/ocular variation as primary conveyors of feeling. Avoid shifting the face on every occasion (which becomes buffoonery); aim instead for natural, judged changes that reinforce the spoken sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching the voice: find and stay within your medium and compass
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Voice ... has its particular Medium and Compass, and the Sweetness of Speech consists in leading it through all the Variety of Tones naturally, and without touching any Extreme. ... 'Leave the Pipe at home, but carry the Sense of this Custom with you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discover your natural vocal range (medium/compass) and cultivate the ability to move through varied tones without straining into extremes. Practice (the anecdote of Gracchus using an ivory pipe) can help fix the proper pitch; internalize that sense rather than rely on external aids. Aim for a flexible but centered voice.
